Jealousy. The painful emotion arising from fear of loss, real or imagined, often coupled with suspicion, possessiveness, and a desire to punish the perceived rival or the beloved. In literature, jealousy is a foundational tragic passion that destroys individuals and societies, turning love into rage and reason into madness.

Jealousy differs fundamentally from envy: jealousy fears loss of what one possesses, while envy desires what another has. In Shakespeare's Othello, jealousy is the driving passion of the entire tragedy. Iago manufactures suspicion with calculated precision, and Othello transforms from a rational general into a deluded murderer consumed by jealous rage. In classical drama, jealousy often appears as divine punishment or the working-out of a curse, as if the gods themselves make mortals jealous to orchestrate their downfall.

Tolstoy's The Kreutzer Sonata takes jealousy as the foundation of sexuality and marriage itself, arguing that possession, suspicion, and violence are inherent in the erotic bond. Psychologically, jealousy threatens identity itself: it reveals the self as contingent, dependent on another's faithfulness, vulnerable to abandonment.

What makes jealousy particularly destructive is that it often escalates without any external cause. Imagination and fear generate evidence of infidelity that has no basis in reality, making jealousy self-fulfilling and cyclical. In modernist literature, jealousy becomes a mode of epistemological anxiety: how can one know another's fidelity or desire? Certainty becomes impossible.
